tasks.content: Silappathikaram (சிலப்பதிகாரம், "The Tale of the Anklet") is one of the ஐம்பெருங்காப்பியங்கள் (Aimperungaappiyangal, Five Great Epics) of Tamil literature, composed by the poet-prince Ilango Adigal (இளங்கோ அடிகள்). Its title comes from சிலம்பு (silambu, an anklet), the object at the heart of its tragic plot. The epic is structured in three books, or காண்டம் (kaandam), each set in the capital of a different ancient Tamil kingdom: புகார்க் காண்டம் in the Chola capital of Puhar, மதுரைக் காண்டம் in the Pandya capital of Madurai, and வஞ்சிக் காண்டம் in the Chera capital of Vanji. At its heart, Silappathikaram is a powerful story about கற்பு (karpu, virtue/chastity) and justice, following the sorrow of a woman named Kannagi.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A வாதம்/விவாதம் (vaadham/vivaadham, debate) is a structured discussion in which speakers argue for or against a given statement, called a தீர்மானம் (theermaanam, motion). To take a clear stance, you might open with "என் கருத்துப்படி..." (en karuthuppadi, "in my opinion...") before stating your position, then give a காரணம் (kaaranam, reason) to support it — for example, "ஏனெனில்..." (yenenil, "because..."). Debaters are generally split into ஆதரவு (aadaravu, those in favour/support) and எதிர்ப்பு (edhirppu, those opposed), and each side takes turns presenting points within a set time. Learning to state an opinion clearly and back it with a reason is the essential first skill of Tamil debate.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Translating between Tamil and English builds a deeper understanding of both languages by forcing you to notice differences in word order and sentence structure. Tamil typically follows a subject-object-verb order, so "நான் பள்ளிக்குச் செல்கிறேன்" (naan pallikku selgiren) word-for-word is "I to-school am-going," which becomes natural English as "I am going to school." Going the other direction, the English sentence "The sky is blue" becomes "வானம் நீலமானது" (vaanam neelamaanadhu) in Tamil, where the verb "is" is expressed through the adjective ending -ானது rather than a separate word. Good translators aim for sentences that sound natural in the target language, not just a literal word-for-word swap.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: யாப்பு (yaappu) is the traditional system of Tamil poetic meter, built from small units that combine into larger ones like building blocks. The smallest unit above a single letter is the அசை (asai, metrical syllable), of which there are two kinds: நேரசை (neerasai, a single long unit) and நிரையசை (niraiyasai, a double short unit). Several asai combine to form a சீர் (seer, metrical foot), several seer combine to form an அடி (adi, a line of verse), and the linking pattern between feet is governed by rules called தளை (thalai). Understanding this ladder — எழுத்து (letter) to அசை (syllable) to சீர் (foot) to அடி (line) — is the foundation for reading and appreciating classical Tamil poetry such as the Thirukkural and Sangam verses.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Studying a novel in depth means tracing how theme, character and historical context interweave across the whole text, not just a single chapter. A character's development often mirrors or challenges a novel's central themes, and understanding when and where a novel was written, its historical context, reveals why certain issues, such as war, class or industrial change, dominate the story. Strong analysis tracks how an author builds a theme gradually, using specific moments and quotations from across the novel rather than relying on a single scene.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Studying a full Shakespeare play means tracking how plot, character and language develop across five acts, not just an isolated extract. Shakespeare often builds character through soliloquy — a speech where a character speaks their inner thoughts alone on stage — revealing motivations the other characters cannot see. Tracing how a character's language changes across the play, in vocabulary, imagery or verse pattern, can reveal their psychological journey, such as a descent into guilt or a rise to power, and understanding the play's structure of acts and scenes shows how tension builds towards its climax.

tasks.content: Poems about war and conflict span many periods and viewpoints, from poems glorifying duty and sacrifice to those exposing the brutal reality of the battlefield, and comparing them reveals how attitudes to conflict have shifted over time and differ between writers. Always support a comparison with precise quotations from both poems, analysed side by side rather than one after the other.

tasks.content: A complex sentence combines a main clause, which can stand alone, with one or more subordinate clauses, which cannot, joined by subordinating conjunctions such as 'although,' 'because,' 'while' or 'since.' Subordination lets a writer show precise relationships between ideas — cause and effect, contrast, or condition — rather than simply listing them with 'and.' Where a subordinate clause is placed matters too: a fronted subordinate clause, at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma, can create emphasis or suspense before the main point arrives.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Every genre carries its own conventions — recognisable features readers expect. Horror relies on building dread through pacing, sensory detail and the unknown; mystery plants clues and red herrings so a reader can almost solve the puzzle alongside the detective; and science fiction extrapolates real science or technology into speculative 'what if' worlds, often to comment on present-day society. Writing convincingly within a genre means deliberately using its conventions — vocabulary, structure, pacing and typical character types — while still creating something original rather than a cliche.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Comparing two non-fiction texts on the same topic means analysing not just what each writer says but how they say it — their tone, structure, evidence and persuasive techniques — and why their viewpoints might differ. Two writers covering the same event might select different facts, use contrasting language, such as neutral reporting versus emotive persuasion, or write for very different audiences and purposes. A strong comparison identifies specific similarities and differences and explains the effect of each writer's choices, rather than simply summarising both texts separately.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Gothic fiction creates unease through atmosphere as much as plot, typically featuring decaying settings, such as crumbling castles or gloomy mansions, oppressive weather, and a sense of the supernatural or uncanny threatening rational order. Writers build tension through pathetic fallacy, where weather reflects mood, foreshadowing, and withheld information that keeps readers uncertain about what is real. Studying a Gothic extract means tracing exactly how setting, structure and word choice combine to unsettle the reader, rather than simply noting 'it's scary.'
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Media literacy means reading news and online content critically, recognising that no source is entirely neutral: headline choice, image selection, which quotations are included, and even word choice, such as 'rioters' versus 'protesters,' can all reveal a publication's bias. Checking a source's ownership, funding and typical audience, and comparing how different outlets report the same story, helps readers spot one-sided reporting and distinguish verified fact from unchecked claims or opinion presented as fact. Being media-literate does not mean distrusting everything — it means questioning and cross-checking before accepting a claim.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A strong argumentative essay states a clear thesis, the writer's central position, in the introduction, then develops distinct points in separate paragraphs, each supported by evidence and explained rather than simply asserted. Acknowledging and rebutting a counter-argument — showing you understand the opposing view before explaining why your position is stronger — makes an argument more persuasive than ignoring it. A confident conclusion restates the thesis in light of the evidence given, without introducing entirely new points.

tasks.content: World literature broadens a reader's understanding beyond the British literary canon, exploring how writers from different countries and cultures use story to explore universal themes — identity, family, conflict, belonging — while also reflecting their own specific cultural and historical context. Reading in translation raises its own questions: a translator makes deliberate choices about word choice, idiom and rhythm, meaning that a translated text carries both the original author's voice and the translator's interpretation. Approaching a text from an unfamiliar culture with curiosity, and researching its context, deepens understanding rather than assuming it works exactly like a familiar British text.
Let's practice what we just learned!

options: context is irrelevant to world literature

it only matters for British texts

tasks.content: Two quantities are in direct proportion if their ratio stays constant, so if y = kx and we know one pair of values we can find k and use it to find others. Two quantities are in inverse proportion if one increases as the other decreases, so xy = k stays constant. For example, if y is directly proportional to x and y = 12 when x = 4, then k = 3, so when x = 9, y = 27.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In a right-angled triangle, Pythagoras' theorem states that a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle). To find the hypotenuse, square both shorter sides, add them, then square root: legs of 3 and 4 give a hypotenuse of the square root of (9 + 16) = the square root of 25 = 5. To find a shorter side, rearrange: square the hypotenuse, subtract the known side squared, then square root.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: A scatter graph shows the relationship between two variables using plotted points. tasks.content: The digestive system breaks down food into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood and used by the body for energy, growth and repair. Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing and saliva start to break down food, continues in the stomach with acid and enzymes, and is completed in the small intestine, where enzymes finish breaking down food and nutrients are absorbed through finger-like projections called villi. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up digestion: amylase breaks down starch into sugars, protease breaks down proteins into amino acids, and lipase breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In a chemical reaction, the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to form new substances called products, with new chemical bonds forming; importantly, atoms are never created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same, which is known as the law of conservation of mass. Many reactions involve an energy change: exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, often as heat, causing the temperature to rise, while endothermic reactions absorb energy, causing the temperature to fall. Chemical reactions can be represented using word equations and balanced symbol equations, which show exactly how many atoms of each element are involved on both sides.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Electric current is the flow of electrical charge around a circuit, measured in amperes (amps, A) with an ammeter, while voltage (potential difference), measured in volts with a voltmeter, is the energy transferred per unit of charge that pushes the current around. Magnets have two poles, north and south, and like poles repel while opposite poles attract, with the invisible magnetic field around a magnet mapped using field lines that run from north to south. An electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field around it, and this effect, called electromagnetism, is used to make electromagnets, which are magnets that can be switched on and off using electricity.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: An ecosystem is made up of all the living organisms (the community) in an area interacting with each other and with the non-living parts of their environment, such as soil, water and climate. Within an ecosystem, organisms depend on one another through feeding relationships shown in food chains and food webs, where energy passes from producers (usually plants, which make their own food by photosynthesis) to primary consumers, then secondary and tertiary consumers. This interdependence means that a change affecting one species, such as a predator being removed, can have knock-on effects throughout the whole food web, which is why maintaining balanced ecosystems is important.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of increasing atomic number, into rows called periods and columns called groups, with elements in the same group sharing similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. Metals, found on the left and centre of the table, are typically shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and malleable, while non-metals, found on the right, are generally dull, brittle if solid, and poor conductors. Group 1 elements, the alkali metals, are very reactive and get more reactive down the group, while Group 0, the noble gases, are extremely unreactive because they already have full outer electron shells.
Let's practice what we just learned!

Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned, contributing to climate change, while most renewable resources produce little or no carbon dioxide during use but can be less reliable, such as solar power depending on sunlight. Choosing energy resources involves weighing up factors like cost, reliability, environmental impact and how much energy each resource can supply.

tasks.content: Light and sound both travel as waves, but light is a transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum (such as space) at very high speed, while sound is a longitudinal wave caused by vibrations, which needs a medium like air, water or a solid to travel through, and travels much more slowly. Waves are described using amplitude (the maximum displacement, related to loudness for sound or brightness for light), wavelength (the distance between two matching points on a wave), and frequency (the number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz), linked by the wave equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Higher frequency sound waves are heard as higher pitch, while for light, higher frequency corresponds to a different colour, towards the violet/blue end of the visible spectrum.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity, called the reactivity series, which helps predict how they will behave in reactions: more reactive metals, such as potassium and sodium, react vigorously, while less reactive metals, such as gold and copper, are largely unreactive. Many metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas (more readily for reactive metals), and react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound in a displacement reaction, which is further evidence used to build up the reactivity series.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food, using energy from light to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen; it takes place mainly in the chloroplasts of leaf cells, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy. Respiration, in contrast, occurs in all living cells and releases energy from glucose for the organism to use; aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, while anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and, in animal cells, produces lactic acid instead. Photosynthesis and respiration are essentially opposite processes, and together they play a key role in maintaining the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Evaluating an investigation means critically reviewing how well the method worked and how confident you can be in the results, rather than simply describing what was done. This includes identifying sources of error, such as random errors (small, unpredictable variations, reduced by repeating measurements and averaging) and systematic errors (a consistent bias, often caused by a fault in equipment such as an incorrectly zeroed balance, which shifts every reading in the same direction). A good evaluation also considers the investigation's reliability (whether repeating it gives consistent results) and validity (whether it actually tests what it claims to, with all other variables properly controlled), and suggests specific, practical improvements.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: புணர்ச்சி (puṇarcci, sandhi) refers to the rules governing how sounds change when two words are joined together in Tamil, similar to how English "do not" becomes "don't." A common example is "மழை" (mazhai, rain) combining with "காலம்" (kaalam, season/time) to form the compound "மழைக்காலம்" (mazhaikkaalam, "rainy season"), where a hard க் sound is inserted at the join. Traditional grammar sorts these changes into categories such as உயிர்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (vowel-to-vowel sandhi), மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (consonant-to-consonant sandhi) and உயிர்மெய்த் தொடர் புணர்ச்சி (mixed sandhi). Recognising sandhi patterns helps you correctly split unfamiliar compound words back into their original parts when reading classical or formal Tamil.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Inbam Pal (இன்பத்துப்பால், also called காமத்துப்பால், Kaamathuppaal) is the third and final section of the Thirukkural, containing 250 couplets across 25 chapters devoted to the theme of இன்பம் (inbam, love). Unlike Aram Pal's ethical teachings or Porul Pal's public-life advice, this section is written as an intimate dialogue between a தலைவன் (thalaivan, hero/lover) and தலைவி (thalaivi, heroine/beloved), exploring courtship, longing, separation and reunion much like the akam poetry of the Sangam tradition. Its verses capture universal emotional experiences of romantic love — the shyness of first attraction, the ache of a lover's absence, the joy of reconciliation — in the same tightly structured two-line kural form used throughout the work. Studying Inbam Pal shows how classical Tamil literature treats love with the same careful craftsmanship as ethics and politics.
Let's practice what we just learned!

levels.levelName: The Jaffna Kingdom: Tamil History in Sri Lanka

tasks.taskName: Lesson: The Jaffna Kingdom: Tamil History in Sri Lanka
tasks.content: Tamil history is not only about mainland India — it also includes a long and proud history in இலங்கை (Sri Lanka). Around the 13th century CE, a Tamil kingdom known as the யாழ்ப்பாண இராச்சியம் (Jaffna Kingdom) was established in the northern part of Sri Lanka, ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty. Its capital was நல்லூர் (Nallur), which became an important center of Tamil Hindu (Saiva) culture, religion, and literature in the island. The kingdom built magnificent temples, most famously the நல்லூர் கந்தசுவாமி கோயில் (Nallur Kandaswamy Temple) dedicated to Lord Murugan, which remains one of the most important Hindu temples in Sri Lanka today. The Jaffna Kingdom traded with South India and other parts of the region, and its rulers supported Tamil scholars and poets, helping Tamil language and culture flourish in the north of the island for several centuries. The kingdom remained independent until 1619, when it was conquered by Portuguese colonizers — bringing an end to centuries of Tamil royal rule in Sri Lanka, though Tamil language, culture, and Hindu traditions continued to thrive among the Tamil community there.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This unit follows the central story of Silappathikaram in detail: Kannagi (கண்ணகி) and her husband Kovalan (கோவலன்) are a young married couple from Puhar, but Kovalan falls for a dancer named Madhavi (மாதவி) and squanders his fortune on her before returning, penniless, to Kannagi. The couple travels to Madurai to rebuild their lives, and Kannagi gives Kovalan her silambu (சிலம்பு, anklet) to sell — but he is wrongly accused of stealing the queen's anklet, which looks similar, and is unjustly executed by order of the Pandya king. Grief-stricken, Kannagi marches to the royal court and proves her husband's innocence by breaking open her remaining anklet: hers contains rubies, while the queen's contained pearls. In her fury at this injustice, Kannagi curses the city of Madurai, and this dramatic episode — Kannagi's grief turning to righteous anger — remains one of the most powerful moments in classical Tamil literature.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Kamba Ramayanam (கம்ப ராமாயணம்), also known as Ramavataram (இராமாவதாரம்), is the celebrated Tamil retelling of the Ramayana epic, composed by the poet Kambar (கம்பர்) around the 12th century CE. While it follows the same core story as Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana — Prince Rama's exile, the abduction of his wife Sita by the demon king Ravana, and the eventual war to rescue her — Kambar reshaped the narrative with rich Tamil poetic style, elaborate imagery and emotional depth suited to a Tamil audience of his era. The work is composed in thousands of verses across multiple kandams (books), and Kambar is often praised as one of the greatest poets in the Tamil literary tradition for the sheer craftsmanship of his verse. Kamba Ramayanam remains one of the most celebrated long narrative poems in Tamil literature, distinct in style and detail from its Sanskrit source.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Writing persuasively about a சமூகப் பிரச்சனை (samoogap pirachanai, social issue) means going beyond simple description to build an argument the reader can be convinced by. Choose a real topic such as சுற்றுச்சூழல் பாதுகாப்பு (environmental protection) or கல்வியின் முக்கியத்துவம் (the importance of education), then open with a clear thesis stating your position on it. Each body paragraph should present one piece of evidence or reasoning — a statistic, an example, or a logical argument — that directly supports that thesis, rather than simply listing loosely related facts. A strong persuasive essay on a social issue also briefly acknowledges an opposing view before explaining why your position remains stronger, which shows the reader you have thought the issue through carefully.

tasks.content: Building on the introduction to debate from Grade 6, this unit practises the formal roles and structure used in a organised Tamil வாதப் போட்டி (vaadhap potti, debate competition). Each side has a முன்மொழிபவர் (munmozhibavar, proposer) who opens the case, and speakers alternate presenting points within a strict கால வரம்பு (kaala varambu, time limit) enforced by a நடுவர் (naduvar, judge/adjudicator). A well-prepared formal debater doesn't just state opinions but organises them into a clear கட்டமைப்பு (kattamaippu, structure) — point, evidence, and a brief rebuttal of the opposing side's likely argument — delivered confidently within the time allowed. Practising this formal structure under timed conditions builds the confidence needed for real competitive debating.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Advanced translation goes beyond simple sentences to tackle idiomatic expressions, where a literal, word-for-word translation would sound strange or lose the original meaning entirely. For example, the Tamil proverb "கிணற்றுத் தவளைக்குக் கடல் தெரியுமா?" should not be translated literally as "does the well's frog know the ocean" but rendered with its equivalent English idiom, "like a frog in a well," to preserve the intended meaning for an English reader. Similarly, translating longer, more complex sentences requires reordering clauses — a Tamil sentence with a relative participle (பெயரெச்சம்) placed before a noun, like "நேற்று வந்த மாணவன்" (the student who came yesterday), must be restructured into an English relative clause with "who," since English cannot place a whole clause directly before a noun in the same way. Skilled translators balance staying faithful to the original meaning with producing natural, fluent sentences in the target language.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Puthukavithai (புதுக்கவிதை, "new poetry") is the modern free-verse movement in Tamil poetry that emerged in the 20th century as a deliberate break from the strict yaappu (poetic meter) rules that had shaped Tamil verse for centuries. Instead of fixed metrical patterns and rhyme, puthukavithai poets write in free verse, using natural rhythms of spoken Tamil, everyday vocabulary and contemporary themes — city life, personal emotion, social commentary — that older classical forms rarely addressed directly. This shift mirrors similar free-verse movements in other world literatures, where poets prioritised emotional directness and thematic freedom over rigid formal constraints. Reading puthukavithai alongside classical Sangam or Thirukkural verse highlights just how dramatically Tamil poetic form has evolved while the language itself remains continuous.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: At the highest level, creative writing is a series of deliberate choices: every word, and every sentence's length and structure, should be chosen for a specific effect rather than habit. Precise verbs and concrete nouns, such as 'the branch snapped' rather than 'something happened,' create sharper images than vague, general language, while sentence length can be manipulated to control pacing — a sudden short sentence after a long, flowing one can land like a physical jolt. Strong writers redraft deliberately, questioning each word choice: does this verb, this rhythm, this structure serve the effect I want the reader to feel?

tasks.content: Transactional writing produces a text with a genuine real-world purpose and audience — a formal letter of complaint, a speech to persuade an audience, or a magazine article to inform and entertain — and each form has its own conventions of layout, tone and structure. A formal letter needs an appropriate greeting, clear paragraphing and a formal sign-off; a speech needs direct address, rhetorical techniques and spoken rhythm; an article needs an engaging headline, byline and a structure suited to its readership. Matching form, register and purpose precisely to the task is central to success in transactional writing.

Other methods include random sampling (every member has an equal chance) and systematic sampling (selecting every nth item from a list).

Real-life graphs such as distance-time graphs also carry meaning: a horizontal section means the object is stationary, and the gradient of a sloped section represents speed.

tasks.content: Genetic information is stored in the nucleus of a cell in structures called chromosomes, made of a molecule called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), which is coiled into a double helix shape; sections of DNA that code for particular characteristics are called genes. Humans have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs in most body cells, having inherited one chromosome of each pair from each parent, while cells divide by mitosis to produce two identical new cells for growth and repair. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, which can have different versions called alleles, and whether a dominant or recessive allele is expressed determines the characteristic (phenotype) an organism shows.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Atoms are made of three types of subatomic particle: protons and neutrons, which have relatively large mass and are found in the central nucleus, and electrons, which have almost no mass and orbit the nucleus in shells (energy levels); protons carry a positive charge, electrons a negative charge, and neutrons no charge, and in a neutral atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons. The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number, which identifies the element, while the total number of protons and neutrons is its mass number. Atoms bond together in different ways: ionic bonding involves the transfer of electrons between a metal and a non-metal to form charged ions that attract each other, covalent bonding involves non-metal atoms sharing pairs of electrons, and metallic bonding involves a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Pressure is the force acting per unit area, calculated with the formula pressure = force ÷ area, and measured in pascals (Pa); this is why a sharp knife (small area) cuts more easily than a blunt one with the same force, and why wide skis spread a person's weight over a larger area to reduce pressure on snow. Pressure in a fluid, such as in a liquid, increases with depth because of the increasing weight of fluid above, and acts equally in all directions at a given point. Newton's laws of motion describe how forces affect movement: an object stays still or moves at a constant speed unless acted on by an unbalanced force (Newton's first law), and the resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, F = ma (Newton's second law).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: The rate of a chemical reaction describes how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed, and can be increased by raising the temperature (giving particles more energy so they collide more often and harder), increasing the concentration of a solution or the pressure of a gas (making collisions more frequent), increasing the surface area of a solid reactant (exposing more particles to collide with), or adding a catalyst, which speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. This is explained by collision theory: for a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy, called the activation energy, and more frequent or more energetic collisions lead to a faster reaction rate. Rate of reaction can be measured experimentally, for example by timing how long it takes for a fixed amount of gas to be produced, or by measuring how a reaction mixture's mass or appearance changes over time.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of the body, such as temperature, water content and blood glucose levels, to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes outside the body. The nervous system detects and responds to changes (stimuli) rapidly using electrical signals: receptors detect a stimulus, sensory neurones carry signals to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), which processes information and sends signals along motor neurones to effectors, such as muscles or glands, which produce a response. A reflex is an automatic, rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought, protecting the body from harm, such as pulling your hand away from something hot.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Electrical power is the rate at which energy is transferred, measured in watts (W), and can be calculated using the equation power = voltage × current (P = V × I); a higher-power appliance transfers more energy every second. In a series circuit, current is the same at every point and the total voltage is shared between components, whereas in a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is the same, but the current is shared between branches, so removing one component does not stop current flowing through the others. Energy transferred by an electrical appliance can be calculated using energy = power × time, which is how domestic electricity bills, based on the number of kilowatt-hours used, are calculated.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-based compounds, most of which are found in or derived from living things or fossil fuels; carbon atoms can form up to four covalent bonds, allowing them to build long chains and rings, giving rise to a huge variety of organic molecules. Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of hydrogen and carbon atoms, and crude oil is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons, most of which belong to a family called alkanes; alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2 and contain only single bonds between carbon atoms, making them relatively unreactive (saturated). Crude oil is separated into more useful fractions, such as petrol, diesel and kerosene, by fractional distillation, which separates hydrocarbons based on their different boiling points.

tasks.content: The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous range of transverse waves, all travelling at the same speed through a vacuum, arranged in order of increasing frequency (and energy) and decreasing wavelength: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Different parts of the spectrum have different uses because of how they interact with matter: radio waves are used for broadcasting, microwaves for cooking and satellite communication, infrared for thermal imaging and remote controls, ultraviolet causes sunburn and vitamin D production in skin, and X-rays and gamma rays, which are the highest-energy, most penetrating waves, are used for medical imaging and treating cancer, though excessive exposure can damage living cells and cause harm such as cancer.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Biodiversity is the variety of different species of living organisms found in an ecosystem or on Earth as a whole, and high biodiversity generally makes ecosystems more stable and resilient to change, because there are more alternative food sources and relationships if one species is affected. Human activities, such as deforestation, pollution, overfishing and climate change, are reducing biodiversity around the world, which is why conservation efforts, including protected nature reserves, captive breeding programmes and controls on hunting or land use, are used to try to protect and restore species and habitats. Ecologists study ecosystems using sampling techniques, such as quadrats to estimate population sizes of plants or slow-moving animals in an area, and transects to see how species distribution changes across an environment.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Survey of Tamil Literary History
tasks.content: Tamil literature spans one of the longest continuous literary traditions in the world, and this unit surveys its major eras in order. It begins with சங்க இலக்கியம் (Sangam literature), the earliest surviving poetry from roughly the last centuries BCE onward, followed by the post-Sangam era of the ஐம்பெருங்காப்பியங்கள் (Five Great Epics), which includes Silappathikaram, Manimekalai, Jivaka Chintamani, Valayapathi and Kundalakesi. Next came பக்தி இலக்கியம் (Bhakti literature), a great flowering of devotional poetry and hymns addressed to Shiva and Vishnu, composed by poet-saints over several centuries of the medieval period. The survey concludes with நவீன இலக்கியம் (modern literature), which grew from the 19th and 20th centuries onward to include novels, short stories and free-verse poetry such as puthukavithai, reflecting contemporary Tamil life and thought.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: செந்தமிழ் (sendhamizh, classical/literary Tamil) and கொடுந்தமிழ் (kodundhamizh, colloquial/spoken Tamil) represent two related but distinct registers of the same language. Classical Tamil preserves older grammatical forms and full spellings closer to traditional rules, as in the literary "செல்கின்றேன்" (I am going), while everyday spoken Tamil often contracts and simplifies this to "போறேன்" in casual conversation. These differences extend beyond single words to sentence structure, vocabulary choices and regional dialect variation, meaning a formal written essay and a casual chat between friends can sound almost like different varieties of the same language. Recognising when to use each register — formal literary Tamil for essays, exams and formal speech, versus natural colloquial Tamil for everyday conversation — is an important skill for any confident Tamil speaker and writer.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Advanced argumentative essay writing builds on basic essay structure by adding an எதிர்வாதம் (edhirvaadham, counter-argument) and பதிலுரை (padhilurai, rebuttal) to strengthen the writer's overall position. After presenting your main thesis and supporting evidence, a strong advanced essay dedicates a paragraph to fairly stating the strongest opposing argument, introduced with a phrase like "சிலர் கருதலாம்..." (some may argue that...), before directly countering it with reasoning or evidence in the rebuttal that follows. This structure — thesis, evidence, counter-argument, rebuttal, conclusion — shows a more sophisticated command of argument than simply repeating one's own view, and mirrors how mature persuasive writing works in any language. A strong concluding paragraph then reasserts the thesis in light of the rebuttal, leaving the reader with a clear, well-supported final impression.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: பொதுப் பேச்சு (podhup pechu, public speaking) and சொற்பொழிவு (sorpozhivu, formal oratory) are valued skills in Tamil culture, where confident, expressive speech has long been prized in gatherings, festivals and civic life. Effective public speaking blends clear content with delivery: varying your pace and tone (குரல் ஏற்ற இறக்கம், voice modulation) to hold an audience's attention, pausing for emphasis before an important point, and using rhetorical techniques such as repeating a phrase for impact. A speaker should also read and adapt to their audience — a school assembly speech calls for a different tone than a formal debate — while maintaining clear, well-organised content throughout, from a strong opening that captures attention to a memorable closing line. Practising aloud, not just writing a speech on paper, is essential to becoming a confident public speaker.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: இலக்கிய விமர்சனம் (ilakkiya vimarsanam, literary criticism) is the practice of analysing a text thoughtfully rather than simply summarising its plot. A literary critic examines கருப்பொருள் (karupporul, theme, the central idea or message a work explores), நடை (nadai, style, the particular way an author uses language and form), and பாத்திரப் படைப்பு (paathirap padaippu, characterisation, how believably and vividly characters are built). Critics also consider the ஆசிரியரின் நோக்கம் (aasiriyarin nokkam, the author's purpose) — why a text was written and what effect it seems designed to have on its reader. Applying these four lenses — theme, style, characterisation and purpose — to a Sangam poem, a Thirukkural couplet or a modern short story reveals layers of meaning that a first, surface-level reading often misses.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Comparative literature places texts from different languages and cultures side by side to notice shared human themes as well as culturally distinct approaches. For example, the Thirukkural's short, universal couplets of ethical wisdom can be compared with Aesop's Fables from ancient Greek tradition — both use compact, memorable forms to teach moral lessons, though the Thirukkural relies on direct statement while Aesop's fables use animal characters and allegory. Similarly, Kamba Ramayanam and an English epic poem like Milton's Paradise Lost can be compared as heroic, morally serious long narrative poems rooted in religious tradition, even though one retells a Hindu epic and the other a Christian one. This kind of comparison sharpens your understanding of each text individually, by asking what is universal about storytelling and morality across cultures, and what is shaped by each culture's particular tradition.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: This capstone grammar unit reviews and connects the major structures studied across earlier years into one advanced picture of Tamil sentence-building. It revisits வேற்றுமை (vetrumai, case markers) that show a noun's role, காலம் (kaalam, tense) that shows when an action happens, and the two participle forms — வினையெச்சம் (adverbial participle, linking sequential actions) and பெயரெச்சம் (adjectival participle, describing a noun) — that let Tamil build complex sentences without separate relative-clause words. It also reviews புணர்ச்சி (sandhi, the rules for sound changes where words join). Seeing all of these features working together in one advanced sentence, such as "நேற்று பள்ளிக்குச் சென்ற மாணவன் இன்று வீட்டில் படித்துக் கொண்டிருக்கிறான்" (the student who went to school yesterday is studying at home today), shows how Tamil grammar builds meaning through layered suffixes and participles rather than many separate small words.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Writing a சிறுகதை (sirukadhai, short story) in Tamil draws on the same core elements as short fiction in any language: பாத்திரம் (paathiram, character), களம் (kalam, setting) and கதைச்சுருக்கம் (kadhaichchurukkam, plot). A strong short story establishes its characters and setting efficiently within the opening lines, then builds a single clear conflict or turning point rather than trying to cram in too many events. Natural-sounding உரையாடல் (uraiyaadal, dialogue) brings characters to life — using colloquial spoken Tamil for dialogue, even within an otherwise more literary narration, often makes characters feel more real and relatable to the reader. Revising your own creative writing by reading it aloud is a useful way to check whether the dialogue and pacing feel natural.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Subramania Bharati: Poet of Freedom
tasks.content: சுப்பிரமணிய பாரதி (Subramania Bharati), affectionately called பாரதியார் (Bharathiyar) and honored as "Mahakavi" (great poet), was born in 1882 in Ettayapuram, Tamil Nadu, and became one of the most important Tamil poets of the modern era. He lived during a time when India was under British colonial rule, and his poetry became a powerful voice for India's freedom movement — he wrote fiery, passionate verses calling for national independence, unity, and courage, and his songs were sung at protests and gatherings across Tamil Nadu. But Bharathiyar wrote about more than just politics: he was also a bold social reformer who used his poetry to speak out against the caste system and to call for the equality and education of women, ideas that were considered very progressive for his time. He wrote beautiful, playful poems for and about children too, such as "சின்னஞ்சிறு கிளியே" (Chinnanchiru Kiliye, "Little Parrot"), which is still taught and loved today. He also composed devotional and patriotic songs about "பாரத மாதா" (Bharat Matha, "Mother India"), blending love of language, faith, and country into his verse. Bharathiyar died young, in 1921, but his poetry continues to inspire Tamil readers, and he is remembered as one of the greatest poets in the history of the Tamil language.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: GCSE English Language Paper 2 asks you to read non-fiction texts, such as articles, letters, speeches, biographies and travel writing, and work out what the writer thinks and how they get their point across. Start by separating explicit information, facts stated directly, from implicit information, ideas the writer suggests without saying them outright. A writer's viewpoint is their overall attitude or opinion on a subject, and you find it by looking closely at word choices. Positive or negative connotations reveal bias: describing a decision as bold and visionary shows approval, while calling it reckless shows criticism. Tone is the writer's attitude expressed through style, and it might be angry, nostalgic, ironic, humorous or urgent. Look for patterns of language across the whole text rather than judging from a single sentence. When you compare two non-fiction texts, focus on both what each writer's viewpoint is and how they present it differently. One writer might use personal anecdotes to build sympathy, while another uses statistics to sound authoritative. Always support your points with a short, well-chosen quotation and explain the effect of specific words or phrases, rather than simply retelling what the text says. Examiners reward analysis of method over summary of content, so keep asking yourself: what has the writer done here, and why might they have done it? Practise annotating texts by underlining strong or unusual words and jotting a one-word note on the effect each creates.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In the fiction reading section of English Language Paper 1, you analyse a short extract from a novel or short story, usually unseen. The key skill is close analysis of language and structure, not simply describing what happens in the plot. When exploring language, identify specific techniques such as metaphor, simile, personification, and sensory imagery, then explain the precise effect each creates for the reader. Do not just name a device: explain why the writer chose it. For example, describing rain as "needles against the window" is a metaphor that suggests sharpness and discomfort, creating a hostile, threatening atmosphere. Structure is equally important and is often under-analysed. Ask how the writer has organised the extract: does it begin with a wide, general description before narrowing to a single character or detail, a technique called a narrative zoom? Does the writer use short sentences to speed up pace during tension, or long, flowing sentences to slow the reader down and build atmosphere? Notice shifts in focus, time, or perspective, and consider why the writer placed information where they did. Always link your analysis back to the question, especially when asked about a specific character, a mood, or a relationship. Use precise subject terminology accurately, such as pathetic fallacy, foreshadowing, or juxtaposition, but only where it genuinely applies. The strongest answers develop a single point in depth with multiple pieces of evidence rather than making many shallow points, so choose your best two or three ideas and explore them fully.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Paper 1 Question 5 asks you to write creatively, either a description based on a picture or an opening to a story. Strong descriptive writing uses varied sentence structures to control pace: short sentences create impact or tension, while longer, complex sentences build detail and atmosphere. Engage more than one sense; instead of only describing what a character sees, include sound, smell, touch or taste to make a setting feel real. Use precise, carefully chosen vocabulary rather than generic adjectives; "the gate groaned on rusted hinges" is more effective than "the gate was old and noisy". Figurative language such as metaphor, simile and personification should be used sparingly but purposefully, each one earning its place by creating a specific effect. In narrative writing, structure matters as much as language. Plan a clear shift or turning point rather than simply describing one continuous scene; even a short extract benefits from a shift in time, focus, or mood. Consider your narrative viewpoint: first person creates intimacy and immediacy, while third person can offer a wider, more controlled view of events. The "show, don't tell" principle is essential: instead of writing "she was scared", show fear through actions, physical sensations and dialogue, such as trembling hands or a held breath. Finally, a strong opening line hooks the reader immediately, and a controlled, deliberate ending, rather than a rushed one, leaves a lasting impression. Always plan briefly before writing so your piece has a clear shape from the very first sentence.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Paper 2 Question 5 asks you to write a transactional text, such as a letter, article, speech or leaflet, to argue, persuade or advise for a specific purpose and audience. Before writing, identify your form, purpose and audience, since these shape your tone, vocabulary and structure. A letter to a newspaper editor needs a more formal register than an article for a school magazine aimed at teenagers. Persuasive writing relies on a toolkit of rhetorical devices, often remembered with the acronym AFOREST: Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Repetition, Emotive language, Statistics, and Triples (a rule of three, such as "safer, cleaner, better"). Rhetorical questions engage the reader directly and make them consider your argument, while direct address, using "you", creates a personal connection. Emotive language appeals to the reader's feelings, but should be balanced with facts or evidence so the writing does not feel one-sided or manipulative. Structure your piece with a clear, engaging opening, a logically ordered middle with one idea per paragraph, and a strong, memorable conclusion, often returning to an idea from the introduction. Use discourse markers such as "furthermore", "however" and "in conclusion" to guide the reader through your argument. Match the correct conventions of form: a speech might include a direct greeting to the audience, a letter needs an appropriate opening and closing, and an article often benefits from a catchy headline and subheadings. Accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar matters throughout, since technical errors distract from even the most persuasive argument.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships
tasks.content: In GCSE English Literature, one cluster of poems in the anthology explores love and relationships, covering romantic love, love within families, loss, and the passage of time within a relationship. When studying these poems, do not memorise the text word for word; instead, understand each poem's central ideas, its form and structure, and a small bank of key quotations you can adapt for different questions. Explore how poets present love through imagery: nature imagery might suggest that love is powerful and natural, while imagery of light and warmth can suggest comfort and joy, whereas imagery of storms or darkness can suggest conflict or danger within a relationship. Consider form: a sonnet's traditional structure, often associated with romantic love, might be used conventionally or subverted to comment on a relationship's difficulty. Look at structural choices too, such as a regular rhyme scheme suggesting harmony, or a broken, irregular rhythm suggesting a relationship under strain. When comparing two poems from this cluster, always compare both similarities and differences in how love or relationships are presented, and in the methods each poet uses to present them. Useful comparison words include "similarly", "in contrast", and "whereas". Context can matter too: a poem written in a different historical period might present ideas about marriage, gender roles or family very differently from a modern poem. Build a personal response supported by evidence, since examiners value genuine interpretation over a rehearsed, generic answer.

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Studying a Prose Text: Themes & Character
tasks.content: For your GCSE prose set text, whether a nineteenth-century novel such as "A Christmas Carol" or "Jekyll and Hyde", or a modern novel, you need a secure understanding of its main themes and how characters are used to explore them. A theme is a central idea the writer explores throughout the text, such as redemption, isolation, ambition, or the tension between good and evil. Characters are not just individuals with a story; they are often built by the writer to represent or embody these themes. When analysing character, avoid simply describing personality traits; instead, explore how the writer presents the character through their actions, speech, appearance and how other characters react to them, and connect this to the text's wider themes and the writer's purpose. Track how a character develops or changes across the novel, since character transformation is often central to a text's meaning, such as a character moving from selfishness towards compassion. Pay close attention to how a writer introduces a key character, since first impressions are carefully constructed and often foreshadow later events. When answering an essay question, always begin with a clear point that directly answers the question, support it with a well-chosen quotation, and then analyse the writer's specific language choices and their effect, before linking your point back to a theme and, where relevant, the writer's intentions or the text's context. Build a revision grid mapping each major character to their key quotations, moments and thematic significance so you can retrieve this information quickly under exam conditions.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Whether your set text is "Macbeth", "Romeo and Juliet" or another play, studying Shakespeare requires understanding both character and theme, alongside an awareness of the conventions of Elizabethan and Jacobean drama. Shakespeare often builds characters through contrast, pairing a character with a foil, another character whose differing qualities highlight their traits, such as a impulsive character set against a more cautious one. Soliloquies, where a character speaks their private thoughts alone on stage, are especially important, since they reveal a character's true motivations, doubts or moral conflict directly to the audience. Pay attention to how language reflects social status and emotional state: characters of high status traditionally spoke in blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, while lower-status characters might speak in prose; a break in a character's usual verse pattern can signal emotional disturbance. Dramatic irony, where the audience knows something a character does not, creates tension and is a technique Shakespeare uses frequently to build suspense. Major themes, such as ambition, fate versus free will, love, revenge or the supernatural, run throughout a play and are explored through multiple characters and plot strands rather than just one. When writing about Shakespeare, always consider the play as a performance intended for a live audience, not only as a written text; think about how a specific line might be delivered, or how staging and imagery would affect an audience watching in the theatre. Link your analysis of character and language to these bigger themes and to the historical and social context of Shakespeare's time.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: Spoken Language forms a separate, non-exam assessment in GCSE English, but the skills it develops, clear presentation, audience awareness and confident speaking, are valuable well beyond the classroom. When preparing a spoken presentation, first consider your purpose: are you informing, persuading, or entertaining your audience? Your purpose shapes your content and tone. Consider your audience carefully too; the vocabulary, formality and examples you choose should suit their age, knowledge and interests. Standard English, using grammatically correct, widely understood language, is expected in formal presentations, while regional dialect or informal register might be used deliberately in casual or storytelling contexts, but should be a conscious choice rather than an accident. Structure your talk clearly: a strong opening that grabs attention, perhaps with a question or a striking fact, a logically organised middle with clear signposting between points, and a memorable conclusion that reinforces your main message. Non-verbal communication matters as much as your words: maintain eye contact to engage your audience, use purposeful gestures rather than fidgeting, and vary your pace, volume and pitch to keep listeners interested and to emphasise key points. Avoid reading directly from a script, since this reduces eye contact and sounds unnatural; instead, use brief cue cards with key words to prompt you. During any discussion or questions afterwards, listen actively, respond directly to what is asked, and adapt your language appropriately to maintain a natural, engaged conversation rather than reciting prepared answers.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: In the unseen poetry section of English Literature Paper 2, you must compare two poems you have never studied before, focusing on how each poet presents a similar idea or theme. This can feel daunting, but the same core skills apply as with any poem: read carefully, identify the central subject and mood, and look closely at language, form and structure. Start by reading both poems twice; the first time for overall meaning, the second time annotating techniques and their effects. Identify what connects the two poems, usually given in the exam question, such as how each poet presents nature, loss, or a relationship, then look for both similarities and differences in how they explore that shared idea. Compare imagery: do both poems use similar types of imagery, such as natural imagery, or does one use light and the other darkness to create contrasting moods? Compare form and structure too: is one poem a tightly controlled sonnet while the other uses free verse with no regular pattern, and what might that structural choice suggest about each poem's content or tone? Always use comparative connectives, such as "similarly", "whereas", "in contrast", and "both poets", to make your comparison explicit rather than writing two separate, unconnected paragraphs. Since you have not studied these poems before, you are not expected to discuss biographical context; instead, focus entirely on what is present in the text itself. Manage your time carefully, since this question usually carries significant marks but should not take longer than the time allocated in your exam plan.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Exam Technique: Language Paper Practice
tasks.content: Success in the English Language papers depends as much on exam technique as on knowledge. Start every exam by reading the instructions and time guidance carefully, and stick to a plan: since marks are usually weighted to match suggested timings, spending too long on a low-mark question risks losing marks elsewhere. Always read the source text or extract closely before attempting any question, underlining or annotating key moments as you go, since strong annotation makes it far easier to find evidence quickly. Pay very close attention to command words in each question, since they tell you exactly what to do: "identify" or "list" requires brief, direct answers with no analysis needed, "explain" requires you to give reasons or effects, and "analyse" or "evaluate" requires detailed exploration of language, structure and effect, ideally with a personal, evaluative judgement. Structure longer answers using a clear method, such as point, evidence, analysis, and effect, sometimes called PEE or PEA, ensuring each paragraph makes one focused point in depth rather than several shallow points. For the extended writing questions, spend a few minutes planning; even a brief plan noting three or four key ideas and their order prevents a disorganised answer. Leave time at the end to check your work for accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar, since technical accuracy contributes to your overall mark, especially on Paper 2's writing question. Finally, never leave a question blank; an attempted answer, even an imperfect one, can earn marks that a blank space never will.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Number: Standard Form, Surds & Indices
tasks.content:
Standard form writes very large or very small numbers as A x 10^n, where 1 <= A < 10 and n is an integer. For example, 320000 = 3.2 x 10^5, and 0.0045 = 4.5 x 10^-3. To multiply numbers in standard form, multiply the A values and add the powers of 10; to divide, divide the A values and subtract the powers. Example: (2 x 10^3) x (3 x 10^4) = 6 x 10^7.

A surd is an irrational root that cannot be simplified to a whole number, such as sqrt(2) or sqrt(5). To simplify a surd, look for the largest square factor. For example, sqrt(50) = sqrt(25 x 2) = sqrt(25) x sqrt(2) = 5sqrt(2). To rationalise a denominator, multiply top and bottom by the surd: 1/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3)/3. Surds add and subtract like terms: 3sqrt(2) + 5sqrt(2) = 8sqrt(2), but sqrt(2) and sqrt(3) cannot combine.

Indices (powers) follow key laws: when multiplying, add powers (a^m x a^n = a^(m+n)); when dividing, subtract powers (a^m / a^n = a^(m-n)); a power of a power multiplies (a^m)^n = a^(mn). A negative index means a reciprocal: a^-n = 1/a^n. A fractional index means a root: a^(1/n) = nth root of a, and a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m. For example, 27^(1/3) = 3, and 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4.

Worked example: Simplify (3 x 10^5) x (2 x 10^-2). Multiply the A values: 3 x 2 = 6. Add the powers: 5 + (-2) = 3. The answer is 6 x 10^3.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content:
To expand two brackets like (x + 3)(x - 5), multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second: x times x = x^2, x times -5 = -5x, 3 times x = 3x, 3 times -5 = -15. Collecting like terms gives x^2 - 2x - 15.

Factorising is the reverse process. For a quadratic x^2 + bx + c, look for two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b. To factorise x^2 + 7x + 12, find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7: these are 3 and 4, so x^2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4). A difference of two squares, like x^2 - 9, factorises as (x - 3)(x + 3), since 9 = 3^2.

When a quadratic is written as ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a not equal to 1, such as 2x^2 + 7x + 3, look for factors of the form (2x + p)(x + q) where p and q multiply to give 3 and combine correctly: 2x^2 + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3).

Once a quadratic is factorised and set equal to zero, each bracket can be set to zero to find the solutions, since if two things multiply to zero, one of them must be zero.

Worked example: Solve x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0. Factorise: two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5 are -2 and -3, so (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0. This means x - 2 = 0 or x - 3 = 0, giving x = 2 or x = 3.

When a quadratic will not factorise nicely, the quadratic formula x = (-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a can always be used instead.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Ratio, Proportion & Rates of Change
tasks.content:
A ratio compares two or more quantities. To share an amount in a given ratio, add the parts to find the total number of shares, divide to find the value of one share, then multiply. Example: share 60 pounds in the ratio 2:3:5. There are 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts, so each part is worth 60 / 10 = 6 pounds. The shares are 2 x 6 = 12, 3 x 6 = 18, and 5 x 6 = 30 pounds.

Direct proportion means two quantities increase together at a constant rate, written y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality. Inverse proportion means one quantity increases as the other decreases, written y = k/x.

A rate of change describes how one quantity changes with respect to another, such as speed (distance divided by time) or density (mass divided by volume). On a distance-time graph, the gradient of the line represents speed; a steeper line means a faster speed, and a horizontal line means the object is stationary.

Compound measures combine two units, like speed in km/h, density in g/cm^3, or pressure in N/m^2. These can be rearranged: speed = distance / time, so distance = speed x time, and time = distance / speed.

Worked example: A car travels 150 km in 3 hours. Find its average speed. Speed = distance / time = 150 / 3 = 50 km/h.

Worked example: y is directly proportional to x. When x = 4, y = 20. Find k and y when x = 7. Since y = kx, 20 = k x 4, so k = 5. When x = 7, y = 5 x 7 = 35.

tasks.content:
Circle theorems describe special angle relationships inside and around circles. The angle at the centre of a circle is twice the angle at the circumference, when both angles stand on the same arc. So if the angle at the circumference is 35 degrees, the angle at the centre is 70 degrees.

The angle in a semicircle is always 90 degrees: if a triangle is drawn inside a circle with one side as the diameter, the angle opposite the diameter is a right angle.

Angles in the same segment are equal: any two angles at the circumference that stand on the same arc are equal to each other.

For a cyclic quadrilateral, a four-sided shape with all corners touching the circle, opposite angles add up to 180 degrees. If one angle is 110 degrees, the opposite angle is 70 degrees.

A tangent is a straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point. The tangent is always perpendicular to the radius at that point, so the angle between them is 90 degrees.

The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment (the angle in the triangle on the other side of the chord).

Worked example: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD has angle A = 95 degrees. Find angle C. Since opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees, angle C = 180 - 95 = 85 degrees.

Worked example: The angle at the centre of a circle is 130 degrees. Find the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc. Since the centre angle is twice the circumference angle, the circumference angle = 130 / 2 = 65 degrees.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Geometry: Trigonometry Beyond Right Angles
tasks.content:
For triangles that are not right-angled, the sine rule and cosine rule let us find missing sides and angles. Label a triangle so that side a is opposite angle A, side b is opposite angle B, and side c is opposite angle C.

The sine rule states a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C). It is used when we know a side and its opposite angle, plus one more piece of information.

The cosine rule states a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos(A). It is used when we know two sides and the included angle (to find the third side), or all three sides (to find an angle, by rearranging).

The area of any triangle can be found using Area = (1/2) x a x b x sin(C), where a and b are two sides and C is the angle between them.

Worked example (sine rule): In triangle ABC, a = 8 cm, angle A = 40 degrees, angle B = 65 degrees. Find side b. Using a/sin(A) = b/sin(B): b = a x sin(B) / sin(A) = 8 x sin(65) / sin(40) = 11.3 cm (to 1 decimal place).

Worked example (cosine rule): In triangle ABC, b = 7 cm, c = 9 cm, angle A = 55 degrees. Find side a. Using a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos(A): a^2 = 49 + 81 - 2(7)(9)cos(55) = 57.7, so a = sqrt(57.7) = 7.6 cm (to 1 decimal place).

Worked example (area): In triangle ABC, a = 6 cm, b = 9 cm, angle C = 70 degrees. Area = 0.5 x 6 x 9 x sin(70) = 25.4 cm^2 (to 1 decimal place).
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content:
Sampling means choosing a smaller group from a whole population to represent it, because surveying everyone is often too slow or expensive. A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen, for example by assigning numbers and using a random number generator. A systematic sample picks members at regular intervals from a list, such as every 10th name. A stratified sample splits the population into groups (strata), such as year groups or genders, and samples from each group in proportion to its size, so the sample reflects the structure of the whole population.

Worked example (stratified sampling): A school has 300 boys and 200 girls, a total of 500 students. A stratified sample of 50 students is needed. The number of boys to sample is 50 x (300/500) = 30, and the number of girls is 50 x (200/500) = 20.

Data can be shown in different ways. A histogram is used for continuous, grouped data with unequal class widths, and the height of each bar is the frequency density, not the frequency. Frequency density = frequency / class width. For example, if a class of width 10 has a frequency of 15, the frequency density is 15/10 = 1.5.

A scatter graph shows the relationship (correlation) between two variables. Positive correlation means both variables increase together; negative correlation means one increases as the other decreases; no correlation means there is no clear pattern. A line of best fit can be drawn through the data to estimate values.

Worked example: A class has width 5 and frequency 20. Frequency density = 20/5 = 4.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Probability: Combined Events & Tree Diagrams
tasks.content:
When two events happen together, we can find combined probabilities using rules or tree diagrams. For independent events (where one event does not affect the other), the AND rule multiplies probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). The OR rule adds probabilities and subtracts any overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).

A tree diagram shows the possible outcomes of two or more events as branches, with probabilities written on each branch. To find the probability of a combined outcome, multiply along the branches. To find the probability of one of several outcomes, add the results of the relevant branches.

When items are removed without replacement, the probabilities change for the second event because the total number of items decreases. This makes the events dependent.

Worked example: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls (8 total). Two balls are picked without replacement. Find the probability both are red. P(first red) = 5/8. Since one red ball has been removed, P(second red) = 4/7. So P(both red) = 5/8 x 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

Worked example: Find the probability of picking one ball of each colour (in either order). This can happen as red-then-blue or blue-then-red: P(R then B) = 5/8 x 3/7 = 15/56. P(B then R) = 3/8 x 5/7 = 15/56. Adding these: P(one of each) = 15/56 + 15/56 = 30/56 = 15/28.

Worked example: For independent events with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5, P(A and B) = 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.2, and P(A or B) = 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.7.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content:
Simultaneous equations are two or more equations that share the same unknowns, and we solve them together to find values that satisfy all equations at once.

For linear simultaneous equations, the elimination method multiplies one or both equations so that the coefficients of one variable match, then adds or subtracts the equations to eliminate that variable. The substitution method rearranges one equation to make a variable the subject, then substitutes it into the other equation.

Worked example (elimination style with substitution): Solve 3x + 2y = 16 and x - y = 2. From the second equation, x = y + 2. Substitute into the first: 3(y + 2) + 2y = 16, so 3y + 6 + 2y = 16, giving 5y = 10, so y = 2. Then x = y + 2 = 4. Check: 3(4) + 2(2) = 12 + 4 = 16, correct.

Simultaneous equations can also involve one linear and one quadratic equation. Substitute the linear equation into the quadratic one to form a single equation, then solve by factorising.

Worked example: Solve y = x + 1 and y = x^2 - 5. Since both equal y, set them equal: x + 1 = x^2 - 5. Rearranging gives x^2 - x - 6 = 0. Factorising: (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 3 or x = -2. Using y = x + 1: when x = 3, y = 4; when x = -2, y = -1. So the solutions are (3, 4) and (-2, -1).

Always check your solutions by substituting back into both original equations.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content:
A vector represents a quantity with both magnitude (size) and direction. Vectors can be written as column vectors, such as (3, 4), meaning 3 units across and 4 units up, or with letters like a and b, often shown in bold.

To add column vectors, add the corresponding components: (2, -5) + (-1, 3) = (2 + -1, -5 + 3) = (1, -2). To subtract, subtract the components: (2, -5) - (-1, 3) = (3, -8). To multiply a vector by a scalar (a number), multiply each component: 2 x (2, -5) = (4, -10).

The magnitude (length) of a vector (x, y) is found using Pythagoras' theorem: magnitude = sqrt(x^2 + y^2). For example, the vector (3, 4) has magnitude sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5.

Two vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other, such as (2, 6) and (1, 3), since (2, 6) = 2 x (1, 3).

A position vector describes the location of a point relative to the origin. If A and B have position vectors a and b, the vector from A to B is written AB = b - a.

Worked example: A point P divides the line AB so that AP:PB = 2:1, where A = (1, 2) and B = (7, 11). The position vector of P is a + (2/3)(b - a) = (1, 2) + (2/3)(6, 9) = (1, 2) + (4, 6) = (5, 8).

Vector proofs often show two vectors are parallel (proving lines are parallel) or that a point lies on a line, by expressing routes between points in terms of given vectors like a and b.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content:
A function is a rule that takes an input and produces exactly one output, often written f(x). For example, f(x) = 2x + 3 means: take x, double it, then add 3. To evaluate f(4), substitute x = 4: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11.

A composite function applies one function to the result of another. If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x^2, then fg(x) means f(g(x)): first apply g, then apply f. fg(x) = f(x^2) = 2x^2 + 1. To find fg(3), first work out g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 1 = 19.

The order matters: gf(x) means apply f first, then g. gf(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)^2. gf(2) = g(f(2)) = g(5) = 25.

An inverse function, written f^-1(x), reverses what f does, undoing the operations in reverse order. To find the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 3, write y = 2x + 3, swap x and y to get x = 2y + 3, then rearrange for y: y = (x - 3)/2. So f^-1(x) = (x - 3)/2.

When sketching graphs, y = x^2 is a parabola with a minimum at the origin, y = x^3 is a cubic curve, and y = 1/x is a reciprocal graph with two branches that never touch the axes. Transformations shift or stretch these graphs: y = f(x) + a moves the graph up by a, and y = f(x - a) moves it right by a.

Worked example: If f(x) = 2x + 3, find f^-1(11). Using f^-1(x) = (x - 3)/2: f^-1(11) = (11 - 3)/2 = 4. Check: f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11, correct.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.content: All living organisms are made of cells, the basic building blocks of life. Animal cells contain a nucleus, which controls the cell and holds genetic material, cytoplasm where chemical reactions happen, a cell membrane that controls what enters and leaves, mitochondria for aerobic respiration, and ribosomes for protein synthesis. Plant cells have all of these plus a rigid cell wall made of cellulose, chloroplasts containing chlorophyll for photosynthesis, and a large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap. Bacteria are prokaryotic cells: much smaller and simpler than animal or plant (eukaryotic) cells, with no nucleus. Instead, bacteria have a single circular loop of DNA, sometimes with extra small rings called plasmids, plus a cell wall, cytoplasm, and cell membrane. Some cells become specialised for a particular job, such as sperm cells (which have a tail and lots of mitochondria), nerve cells (long and thin to carry electrical impulses), and root hair cells (with a large surface area for absorbing water). Unspecialised cells that can develop into different cell types are called stem cells. Scientists study cells using microscopes. Light microscopes are cheaper and can be used on living samples, but electron microscopes use beams of electrons to give much higher magnification and resolution, revealing tiny structures like ribosomes and mitochondria in detail. Magnification is calculated using the formula magnification equals image size divided by actual size, and measurements are usually given in millimetres (mm), micrometres (μm), or nanometres (nm), where 1 mm = 1000 μm.
Let's practice what we just learned!

tasks.taskName: Lesson: Biology: Organisation - Digestive & Circulatory Systems
tasks.content: The digestive system breaks down large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. Digestion starts in the mouth, where amylase begins breaking down starch into sugars. Food then passes down the oesophagus into the stomach, which churns food and adds hydrochloric acid and the protease enzyme pepsin to begin digesting protein. The liver produces bile, which is stored in the gall bladder before being released into the small intestine; bile neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats, breaking them into tiny droplets to increase their surface area for lipase to act on. The pancreas also releases amylase, protease, and lipase into the small intestine. Digested food is absorbed in the small intestine, which is lined with finger-like villi that greatly increase surface area for absorption. Undigested material passes into the large intestine, where water is reabsorbed. The circulatory system transports substances such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nutrients around the body. The heart has four chambers: the right atrium and right ventricle pump deoxygenated blood to the lungs, while the left atrium and left ventricle pump oxygenated blood to the rest of the body, making humans a double circulatory system. Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure and have thick, muscular walls; veins carry blood back to the heart and contain valves to prevent backflow; capillaries are one cell thick, allowing efficient exchange of substances with tissues. Blood itself is made of red blood cells (carrying oxygen using haemoglobin), white blood cells (fighting infection), platelets (helping blood clot), and plasma (the liquid that transports everything).
Let's practice what we just learned!
